rules_text:
For some unknown reason, we now find ourselves in a situation where we must quickly interpret a six-digit digital code. We will analyze this code by gathering various uncertain pieces of information. Its meaning will become clear in our hands, just as it always has.

In Digit Code, each player in a two-player game creates a secret six-digit code, with three numbers above three numbers, with a digit 0-9 appearing at most twice and not adjacent to one another. The letters A-Y are used to indicate number segments in a column or in a row, or within a particular digit. Players take turns asking each other questions of the following four types:


     How many spaces in row ? or column ? are filled?
     Is the number ? even or odd?
     Looking at the adjacent numbers ? and ??, which one is larger?
     Is the segment at row ? and column ?? filled?


Each player must ask all four question types before they can repeat a question type. On a turn, a player can give a six-digit number instead of a question. If they have guessed all six numbers correctly, they win; if not, the opponent says "Wrong", and the game continues. If a player guesses incorrectly twice, they lose.

With three or more players, one player creates a six-digit number that the other players race to deduce first, with the players asking questions in turn. Once again, if a player guesses incorrectly twice, they are out of the game.

[Rating: 3/10] obsolete due to Turing Machine and even though it is a neat game idea it lacks of interesting choices or thrill. you could (and probably will) play the same algorithm every time except the endgame of course. and i played the digital version...

[Rating: 3/10] It’s hard to see why you would want to play this. It’s not interesting to ‘deduce’ the segments of an LED number and there’s very limited logic to put into play here - for the first many turns you are going to follow a standard algorithm and then just mop up the leftovers. Played on BGA; pretty sure it would be much worse physically.

[Rating: 3/10] No enjoyment in this game. In majority of the games you and/or the opponent end up with a 50% guess at the code.

[Rating: 4/10] Yuck. This felt like a really bad logic puzzle. Unlike Gamme Logic which felt like cute logic puzzles.

[Rating: 5/10] Essentially gamer battleship/guess who, where you are trying to deduce a 6 digit number. It was interesting but nothing that really hooked me.

[Rating: 5/10] As every other logical game (other examples are "It's a bomb", "Turing machine", "Mastermind", etc.) this game only relies on logical skills and luck.  If players with different logical skills are playing against each other, the most skilled will ALWAYS win. If all players are skilled, it will just be a matter of luck. If none is so skilled, it will just be a matter of luck. So this game is actually boring.  It's the kind of game that you may find printed in a puzzle magazine, not in a physical version as a real boardgame. Disappointing.

[Rating: 5/10] Actually a nice concept for a game, but when literally all information is public, it's just about someone seeing the solution first or someone asking a question that revealed the last number. There has to be some private information in a deduction game.
